items.topic: Settings relocation: dialog vs. slide-over panel
items.context: The SettingsPage is ~558 lines with 5 card sections, a save button, navigation blocker, and unsaved-changes guard. Moving it to a non-page context requires choosing between a modal dialog (centered overlay) and a slide-over panel (right-side drawer). Dialog is simpler to implement and more familiar for 'edit & save' workflows. Slide-over preserves dashboard context behind it but adds layout complexity and may feel awkward on mobile.

options.label: Modal dialog (centered, full-width on mobile)
options.rationale: Simpler implementation, familiar save-and-close pattern, works well with existing navigation blocker. Recommended because settings is an infrequent operation that doesn't need dashboard context visible.

options.label: Slide-over panel (right drawer)
options.rationale: Dashboard stays visible behind panel, feels more 'app-like'. However, adds overlay/z-index complexity, requires separate mobile treatment, and settings content is long enough to need its own scroll context.

options.label: Keep settings as a route but remove from tab bar
options.rationale: Least change — settings page stays as-is, gear icon just navigates to /settings. Dashboard gets the tab slot. Loses the 'quick access' feel but avoids dialog complexity.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: Currently '/' redirects to '/backlog'. With the new Dashboard tab, it could become the default landing page. The dashboard provides a high-level overview which is useful for orientation, but power users who live in the backlog may find the extra click annoying.

options.label: Dashboard is the default landing page ('/' → '/dashboard')
options.rationale: Natural 'home' page pattern. Director team and occasional users get immediate system health overview. Recommended because the dashboard is designed as the entry point for understanding system state.

options.label: Backlog remains the default ('/' → '/backlog')
options.rationale: Power users skip the overview and go straight to work. Dashboard is accessible via tab but not forced.

options.label: User-configurable default page (setting)
options.rationale: Flexibility, but adds complexity and a setting that most users won't change.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: Some backlog items have no initiative. The dashboard is initiative-centric, so unassigned items could be invisible. Options range from a simple count/link to a dedicated pseudo-card.

options.label: Stat in the stats bar + 'Unassigned' pseudo-card in the initiative grid
options.rationale: Most visible. Pseudo-card looks like an initiative card but labeled 'Unassigned' with its own rollup. Makes unassigned items first-class. Recommended because it ensures nothing is hidden and uses the same visual language as initiative cards.

options.label: Count badge in the stats bar only (clickable to filter backlog)
options.rationale: Minimal — doesn't clutter the initiative grid. Users click the badge to see unassigned items in the backlog view.

options.label: Separate section below initiative cards
options.rationale: Visually distinct from initiatives. Shows a compact list of unassigned items rather than a card.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Needs Attention feed: data source strategy
items.context: The 'Needs Attention' feed aggregates items needing human action from multiple sources: failed executions, unresolved workshop decisions, needs_fixup items, and pending prompt-manager decisions. This data spans multiple API domains (execution, backlog/workshop, prompt-manager). The question is whether to create a dedicated API endpoint or compose client-side from existing queries.

options.label: Dedicated backend endpoint: GET /api/v1/dashboard/attention
options.rationale: Single request, server computes the aggregation. Cleaner data contract, easier to paginate. However, requires new API work (out of scope for UI-only research).

options.label: Client-side composition from existing endpoints
options.rationale: Use existing endpoints (runs list filtered by failed, backlog items with pending questions, items in needs_fixup status) and merge client-side. No new backend work needed for the initial implementation. Recommended because it aligns with the UI-scoped acceptance_allow and lets us iterate on the feed shape before committing to a backend contract.

options.label: Hybrid: use existing endpoints now, add dedicated endpoint later
options.rationale: Start with client-side (B) and document the ideal backend contract for future implementation. Best of both worlds but requires discipline to actually build the backend endpoint.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: The spec calls for a 1-10 priority scale for initiative sorting. The current backlog items use a simple 1-5 priority. Using a different scale for initiatives could cause confusion, but 1-10 provides finer granularity for the director team to rank competing initiatives.

options.label: 1-10 scale as specified, default 5
options.rationale: Finer granularity for director team ranking. Different from backlog item priority (1-5) but initiatives are a different abstraction level. Recommended because the director team needs more nuance when prioritizing across many initiatives.

options.label: 1-5 scale matching backlog items, default 3
options.rationale: Consistency with existing priority system. Simpler mental model. May be insufficient for ranking 10+ initiatives.

options.label: Free-form integer (no fixed scale), sorted ascending
options.rationale: Maximum flexibility, but no visual semantics (what does '47' mean?). Harder to design consistent badge/indicator UI.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.text: The existing InitiativeRollup already includes total, completed, in_progress, failed, and pending counts — this maps directly to the initiative card progress bar and status dots. No new rollup fields are needed for the basic card design.

The RollupStatus has a 'failed' field (not 'blocked' as described in the spec). The backlog item statuses that feed into this are: backlog, ready, in_progress, needs_review, needs_fixup, completed, failed. The card design should use 'failed' rather than 'blocked' to match the actual data model, or we need to clarify whether 'blocked' means 'has unresolved dependencies' (a different computation from the dep graph).

plan_updates: Created initial plan scaffold with all 13 mandatory sections. Sections 1-6, 8, 11-13 have substantive content. Sections 7, 9, 10 are TBD pending workshop decisions. Documented current technical context including initiative model fields, navigation structure, settings page complexity, and existing rollup data shape.
